newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba blames people from U.S. for hotel explosions.
newsitem.headline: Cuba blames people from U.S. for hotel explosions.

text.p: Cuba's Interior Ministry on Saturday blamed people from the United States for bombing two Havana hotels in attacks that injured three people and damaged the hotels' lobbies.
"The Interior Ministry has evidence that the people responsible for these deeds and also the materials they used came from the United States," said a brief ministry statement read on state radio.

The statement said the explosions that rocked the lobbies of the Hotel Nacional and the Hotel Capri within minutes of each other around 11:35 a.m. local time (1535 GMT) on Saturday were caused by "explosive artifacts."
It said they slightly wounded three people and caused damage to windows and furniture in the two hotels.
The statement did not give any further information. It did not say if anyone had been arrested in connection with the explosions.
The brief statement gave no indication of specific people suspected of being responsible for the explosions or what sort of evidence the Interior Ministry had.

However, official suspicion would be likely to fall on hardline exile opponents of Castro in Florida, some of whom have carried out violent protests in the past. In 1991, a Miami exile group claimed responsibility for a seaborne machinegun attack on a hotel at the beach resort of Varadero.
Asked soon after the explosions what he thought caused them, Tourism Minister Osmany Cienfuegos, visiting the hotels shortly after the blasts, said: "Obviously they are enemies of ours."
The Nacional and Capri hotels are about 200 yards (metres) apart in Havana's central Vedado district and the explosions went off within minutes of each other.
Cienfuegos said the explosion at the Capri was in a sofa and there were no injuries at that hotel.
Danish tourist Ole Madsen and several hotel workers at the Nacional said three people were slightly injured there.

The director of Havana's Calixto Garcia hospital, Armando Guerra, said two people were treated at his hospital, one Jamaican and one Cuban. They were not seriously hurt and were discharged after treatment for cuts, Guerra said.

A security cordon of police and plainclothes security officials prevented reporters from entering the Nacional, a luxury hotel and a landmark on the Havana skyline owned and managed by the state Cuban firm Gran Caribe.
Madsen, who was sitting in the Hotel Nacional garden at the time of the explosion, said the blast appeared to have ripped through a row of telephone booths in the lobby.
He said that ground floor windows opening onto the back of the hotel were broken.
Many ground floor windows were shattered by the blast at the Capri, a 1950s highrise building owned and managed by Cuban state firm Horizontes.

"We heard a very loud noise, like an earthquake," said Spanish tourist Carlos Alvarez, from Lugo, describing the explosion at the Capri. "In the lobby there was horrible confusion and hysteria; everyone was crying," he added.
Pascal Massiot, a Frenchman from Nantes, said he was convinced the explosion was a bomb and surprised that violence had apparently hit Cuba. He added "there were a lot of people in a state of shock".
Saturday's explosions followed reports in U.S. news media that a small bomb exploded in the discotheque of Havana's Hotel Cohiba in mid-April, causing damage but no injuries.

President Fidel Castro's Communist government never confirmed or denied that report. The Spanish hotel chain Sol Melia, that manages the Cohiba Hotel, said at the time there was an explosion at the disco, but it was caused by faulty gas piping.
Violence involving firearms or explosives is rare in Cuba. The tourist industry is the leading source of hard currency for the cash-strapped island and Cuba is anxious to present a clean, safe image.
The atmosphere near the hotels immediately after Saturday's explosions was tense, with plain clothes security officials trying to stop foreign cameramen from filming the scene.
